'''Gaussian distribution on a locally compact Abelian group''' is a generalization of the classical  
[[Normal distribution|normal distribution]]. Roughly speaking, it extends the concept of a normal distribution from the [[Euclidean space]]  to more general topological groups, i.e., when the group is <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, it coincides with the usual [[Multivariate normal distribution|multivariate normal distribution]].  
It was introduced by Kalyanapuram Rangachari Parthasarathy, Ranga Rao, and Srinivasa R. S. Varadhan in 1963<ref name=PRV1>K. R. Parthasarathy, R. Ranga Rao, S. R. S. Varadhan. ''Probability distributions on locally compact abelian groups'', Illinois Journal of Mathematics, 7 (1963), pp. 337–369. doi:10.1215/ijm/1255644642</ref>, see also <ref name=P1>K. R. Parthasarathy. ''Probability measures on metric spaces''. New York; London: Academic Press, 1967.</ref>.
This distribution plays an important role in the representation of characteristic functions of infinitely divisible distributions<ref name=PRV1/>, the arithmetic of probability distributions<ref name=F2>G. M. Feldman. ''Arithmetic of probability distributions and characterization problems on Abelian groups''. Transl. Math. Monographs, Vol. 116. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society, 1993. {{ISBN|978-0-8218-4568-6}}</ref>, and in characterization problems of mathematical statistics on locally compact Abelian groups<ref name=F3>G. Feldman. ''Characterization of Probability Distributions on Locally Compact Abelian Groups''. Mathematical Surveys and Monographs, Vol. 273. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society, 2023. {{ISBN|978-1-4704-7295-5}}</ref>.

== Definition ==

Let <math>X</math> be a second countable locally compact Abelian group, let <math>Y</math> be its character group, and let <math>(x,y)</math> denote the value of a character <math>y \in Y</math> at an element <math>x \in X</math>.

A probability distribution <math>\gamma</math> on the group <math>X</math> is called Gaussian if its characteristic function ([[Fourier transform]]) is of the form

<div class="center">
<math>
\hat{\gamma}(y) = (x,y)\exp\{-\varphi(y)\},
</math>
</div>

where <math>\varphi</math> is a continuous non-negative function on <math>Y</math> satisfying the functional equation

<div class="center">
<math>
\varphi(u+v)+\varphi(u-v)=2\bigl[\varphi(u)+\varphi(v)\bigr], \quad u,v\in Y.
</math>
</div>

A Gaussian distribution is called symmetric if <math>x = 0</math>. 

== Properties ==

1. A Gaussian distribution is [[Infinitely divisible distribution#Infinitely divisible distribution on locally compact Abelian groups|infinitely divisible]]<ref name=PRV1/>.

2. The support of a Gaussian distribution is a coset of a closed connected subgroup of <math>X</math><ref name=PRV1/>.

3. A symmetric Gaussian distribution is a continuous homomorphic image of a Gaussian distribution on a linear space (either finite-dimensional <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> or infinite-dimensional <math>\mathbb{R}^\infty</math>, the space of all sequences with [[product topology]])<ref name=F1>G. M. Feldman. ''Gaussian Distributions on Locally Compact Abelian Groups''. Theory of Probability and Its Applications, 23 (1979), pp. 529–542. doi:10.1137/112306</ref>.

4. Let <math>X</math> be connected. If <math>X</math> is not [[locally connected space|locally connected]], then every Gaussian distribution on <math>X</math> is [[singular measure|singular]] with respect to the [[Haar measure]]  on <math>X</math>, whereas if <math>X</math> is locally connected and finite-dimensional, then any Gaussian distribution on <math>X</math> is either [[Absolute continuity|absolutely continuous]] or singular with respect to the Haar measure on <math>X</math><ref name=F1/>. The corresponding question for infinite-dimensional locally connected groups remains open, although both types of Gaussian distributions on such groups can be constructed.

5. On finite-dimensional connected groups, any two Gaussian distributions are either mutually absolutely continuous or mutually singular<ref name=F1/>.
